title: Automating onboarding checklist without losing the relationship
metaTitle: Client onboarding as a short checklist
excerpt: Run week one as a short checklist with named owners. A person sends the welcome and checks access before any client sees the wrong files.
alt: A white modernist building with stacked cubic volumes and tall windows against a pale sky. Onboarding is the front door: a checklist, then a person who checks the keys.
caption: The front of the building. Week one is the door. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs on a week-one onboarding list?
faqs.answer: The decision-maker's name, where files live, the specific files you need, the kickoff, and how you will communicate. Each item needs an owner with a name. A forty-item template copied from a larger firm will be abandoned by Wednesday.

faqs.question: Can the welcome email send itself?
faqs.answer: A person should send it, or release a template filled only with names and dates from the record. Access invites need a person on the first projects, because the wrong folder is hard to undo. Do not add a payment in that sequence that was not already agreed.

faqs.question: When should the onboarding sequence stop?
faqs.answer: When the list is done, or when the client is not ready and a person moves the date. A sequence that cannot pause will keep asking for a kickoff that happened, or for one that should not happen yet. Closed lists are part of the design.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Client onboarding automation should walk a new client through week one as a checklist with owners, not as a sequence of cheerful emails that pretend the work has started. Access, files, and the name of the person who decides: those are the items. A bot that welcomes them into a relationship you have not set up will create the first mess.

Automate the handoff around that first week. The machine may create the tasks, remind the studio, and fill a welcome note from facts you already collected. Keep a person on anything the client will see, anything they are asked to pay, and anything you cannot undo, especially a folder shared with the wrong people. Time the minutes of chasing missing logins against the minutes of checking the list before it goes out.

## The list is the product of week one

Write the checklist before kickoff, at the size you will actually finish. A forty-item template copied from a larger agency will be abandoned by Wednesday. A short list that names the real gates will be used.

- Who decides, and who else should be copied.
- Where files live, and who has access on both sides.
- The brand or product materials you need before design can start, stated as specific files, not "any brand assets."
- The kickoff: when it is, who attends, what they should bring.
- How you will communicate, and what a same-week reply means in practice.

Each item has an owner. Some owners are on your side. Some are on theirs. "The client" is not an owner. A name is. If you do not know the name yet, the first item is to learn it, and a person asks.

Hanabi's client portal is the place brand files, documents, and updates live after delivery, and it is a sane place for them during the work too. Week one can include "you can open the portal" only after a person has confirmed the access is theirs and not another client's. Sharing the wrong workspace is the mistake you cannot politely undo, because they may see someone else's files.

## What the machine may set up

On the day the project is allowed to start, the workflow can create the internal tasks, the folder skeleton, and the dates. It can assign the studio-side owners you already named. It can draft the welcome note from the project name, the decision-maker's name, and the kickoff time, using a template you wrote.

It can remind your own team when an item is still open the day before kickoff. That reminder is internal. It can be direct. A reminder to the client is a different object, because they will see it.

Do not let the workflow invite a list of emails it found in a signature or a previous thread. Access is a list a person checks. One extra address on a brand folder is a disclosure. Build the invite from the names you wrote down at the start of the engagement, and have a person press it the first several times.

Do not let it send a payment request that was not already agreed. Week one often includes an invoice, and that invoice follows the rule you use for any bill: the amount comes from the agreement, and a person releases the note. Onboarding is not a back door that adds a fee for "setup."

Do not let it book a kickoff onto calendars beyond the people who already accepted a time. Proposing a time in the welcome note is enough. Holding a time the founder did not offer will start the work with an apology.

## The note the client actually receives

The welcome note is short. It says who their contact is, what you need from them and by when, where to put files, and when you will talk. It does not recap your whole process, and it does not ask them to read a twelve-page guide before they are allowed to begin. A link to one page is fine if that page is the checklist itself.

A person sends it, or a person releases a template that has been filled only with names and dates from the record. A model does not add a paragraph about how excited you are to transform their business. They have already decided to work with you. Excitement in week one is competence: the access works, the ask is clear, the kickoff has an agenda of questions rather than a performance.

If a file is missing, the reminder names the file. "Just checking in on onboarding" is how a founder with a company to run learns to ignore you. "We still need the logo pack, or we will start with type only, and here is what that means" is a reminder a person can stand behind. The consequence, if there is one, is something you will actually do, written by a person.

People will not study a long welcome. Nielsen Norman Group's [How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is the research to keep in mind: users often leave a page in 10 to 20 seconds, and they read only about a quarter of the text. Your checklist should make sense in that first glance. The decisions and the missing files go at the top. The philosophy of your process does not go in at all.

## Access, money, and other hard-to-undo steps

Confirm access by opening it the way the client will, with a person watching the first projects. A screenshot of permissions is not the same as a client who can upload. The workflow can mark the task done only after that check, not when the invite was sent. Sent is not received, and received is not usable.

Revoking a wrong share is the emergency path, and a person does it as soon as they notice, then tells the affected clients what happened if their files were exposed. Do not wait for a postmortem template. The automation's job after an incident is to stop inviting anyone else until the list is clean.

Contracts and change requests do not ride along inside the welcome sequence. If the scope is not signed, the checklist should not pretend the kickoff is a design meeting. A person pauses the sequence. A machine that "keeps momentum" by starting anyway will produce work the client has not agreed to pay for, which is an undo problem for both of you.

[Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) shows the kind of shipped sites and products this first week is meant to protect. The checklist is how that work starts with the right files and the right people in the room.

## Minutes saved against minutes of review

Time five onboardings done by hand. Include the forgotten login, the kickoff that started without the brief, and the email you rewrote three times. That is the chore.

Time the new path. Reviewing the filled welcome note, checking the access list, and releasing reminders. Add the repair time when a client gets the wrong file, the wrong price, or a second conflicting instruction from an old template. If repair shows up at all in the first month, a person releases every client-facing note until you know why.

The internal reminders should be the bulk of the savings. You stop being the only person who remembers that the font files were not in the folder. The client-facing mail should get shorter, not more frequent. If they are receiving more email than before, the automation is performing busyness.

Count kickoffs that start ready: the right people, the files, the questions. That count is the result. A finished checklist with a confused client is not.

## After week one

Close the onboarding list when the items are done, and move the project to the ordinary rhythm of the work. Leave the workflow running and it will keep asking for a kickoff that already happened. Closed lists are a feature.

What carries forward is the same home for files and the same named approver. When a new stakeholder joins later, a person adds them. The original automation does not watch the company forever and invite new staff it notices in an email. That watch is a surveillance habit dressed up as help.

If week one slips because the client is not ready, say so and move the date. Do not send the day-three and day-five notes as if the kickoff had happened. A sequence that cannot pause is a sequence that will lie.

Write the checklist down where the next project can reuse it, and remove any item you skipped on the last two projects. The list should get more honest over time, not longer. A studio that adds a step after every scare, and never removes one, will automate a process nobody finishes.

Keep a note of which items slipped on the last three projects. If the same file is always late, the checklist is asking for it too early, or you are asking the wrong person. Change the owner or the day. A list that repeats the same miss is not a process. It is a wish. Fix it before you automate the reminder, or you will simply send the wish on a schedule.

Once the client is in motion, they will expect a rhythm of news. [Automating report sending without losing the relationship](/blog/automating-report-sending-without-losing-the-relationship) is the piece to read next, because a weekly number they already expect is a gift when it is true and a breach when a failed fetch goes out as a zero.
